characters: Bawa: a seven-year-old Ghanaian boy with short hair wearing a comfortable yellow-and-blue patterned cotton shirt and dark shorts.
Napari: his calm ten-year-old sister with neat braided hair wearing a coral-orange dress, holding a small silver hand torch.
Their mother: a warm Ghanaian woman in an indigo-and-gold wrapper cloth and headwrap sitting reassuringly with her children.

narrationPlan.voice: A small, worried boy’s voice for Bawa; a calm older sister’s voice for Napari
narrationPlan.pace: Hushed at first, then warm and calm (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A quiet night tune with crickets, then a gentle lift when the lights return (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Power cuts are common in many communities. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on sources of light (B2.2.1.2.1) and on safety with electricity (B3.4.1.1.1).
The sister’s voice gives clear rules: stay calm, use a torch not a flame, never touch a fallen wire, tell a grown-up.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the light facts: light from a source bounces off objects to our eyes.
Check the safety messages match local electricity-safety guidance.

teacherGuide.overview: A power cut shows children which things give light, how we see objects, and how to stay calm and safe. Based on NaCCA Science standards on sources of light and safety with electricity.
learningGoals: Say two safety rules for a power cut.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (NaCCA B2.2.1.2.1, B3.4.1.1.1)
subjectLinks.link: Sources of light and safety with electricity

beforeReading: Ask: what do you do when the lights go out at home?
whileReading: Dim the room and shine a torch on a toy to show how we see.
afterReading: Make a safety card: use a torch, stay calm, tell a grown-up.
Sort pictures into things that give light and things that do not.
discussion: Why is a torch safer than a candle for children?
How can we help a younger child who is afraid of the dark?
reflection: What helps you feel calm in the dark?

support: Use picture cards: torch, bulb, sun, stone.
stretch: Say why the moon looks bright even though it does not make its own light.

culturalNotes: Power cuts are common in many communities. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on sources of light (B2.2.1.2.1) and on safety with electricity (B3.4.1.1.1).
The sister’s voice gives clear rules: stay calm, use a torch not a flame, never touch a fallen wire, tell a grown-up.
localiseThis: Use the light sources found in your area: torch, lantern, phone light.
Never let children play with matches, candles or fallen wires.
